summary: SkillMutator generates malicious Agent Skills whose harmful behavior emerges from SKILL.md instructions steering otherwise innocuous helper scripts (13 attack categories), iteratively refining mutations against rule-based, commercial and LLM scanners. Existing scanners detect few such mutations; the authors distill GPT-5.4 four-phase security-analysis traces into a LoRA-tuned Qwen2.5-Coder-7B scanner that reaches 88.2% detection on the 76-scenario GPT-5.4-oracle set and 82.5% accuracy (8% FPR) on 200 ClawHub marketplace skills.

claims.claim: Open-source and commercial skill scanners detect only 2-8% and 9-17% of cross-modal attacks
claims.evidence: Table IV: skill-security-scan 2.1/6.4/7.9%, Snyk Agent Scan 16.7/9.5/9.2% (n=48/63/76). Mutations were refined specifically to evade these two scanners with their rule taxonomy exposed (§IV-C), which the authors concede makes these lower bounds under adaptive evasion. SkillScan (held out) 0-1.3%.

claims.claim: Distilled 7B scanner improves detection from 17.1% to 88.2%, surpassing GPT-4o-mini (23.7%) and GPT-5.4-mini (79.0%) and reaching GPT-5.4 (86.8%)
claims.evidence: §VI-D, Fig. 6: 67/76 vs GPT-5.4 66/76 (a one-scenario difference, no CIs). Under a Claude-Opus-4.7 judge 85.5% vs 81.6%. Training mutations are generated by the same GPT-5.4 oracle pipeline (different source skills), so the student is in-distribution while baselines are not; deterministic refinement and prefill choices appear to be selected on the same 76-item evaluation set (Table VI).

claims.claim: The scanner has acceptable false-positive behavior
claims.evidence: Table XI per-category metrics: precision 60.9%, specificity 80.5% (43 false positives) on unmodified Anthropic skills; ClawHub Table VII: FPR 8.0% on 100 clean skills, LOW/MED tier accuracy only 60-68%. Precision of frontier baselines not reported, so the comparison is recall-only.
claims.location: App. B-B Table XI, §VI-E Table VII

claims.claim: Local scanner has the lowest cost per detected attack ($0.00469)
claims.evidence: Table VIII; local A100 cost assumptions vs API pricing.

patterns.note: On-demand skills (SKILL.md + scripts) are a supply-chain attack surface that current scanners miss; loading third-party skills needs vetting.
Off-the-shelf prompt-injection detectors (LLM-Guard 4.0%, PIGuard 17.1%, DataSentinel 10.5% on GPT-5.4 set) fail; a task-specific distilled scanner does much better on in-distribution attacks.
LLM scanners outperform rule-based ones, and LLM judges (GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.7) score detections; judges cross-checked against each other but not humans.
Install-time gating of skills as a policy control.
Rule-based SAST/SCA skill scanners detect <=17% of adaptive cross-modal attacks.

methodology.sample: Eval: 17 official Anthropic skills mutated into 48/63/76 evaluable attacks by three oracles; train: 1,219 GPT-5.4 mutations of 68 community skills; in-the-wild: 200 ClawHub skills (100 clean, 100 suspicious)
methodology.baselines: skill-security-scan, Snyk Agent Scan, SkillScan, LLM-Guard, PIGuard, DataSentinel, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-5.4-mini, GPT-5.4, base open-weight models
methodology.models: Students: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, Llama, Mistral, Gemma variants; teacher/oracle/judge GPT-5.4; second judge Claude Opus 4.7
methodology.variance: None; single runs, no CIs on n=76
methodology.ablations: Phase-by-phase schema ablation (Table VI), prefill per model family, stealth-aware selection, iterative refinement
methodology.contamination_controls: Source-level separation of training (community) and evaluation (Anthropic) skills; same oracle family generates both
methodology.languages: Skill scripts (mostly Python/shell) and natural-language SKILL.md

standards.artifacts: Prompts in appendix; mutated skills only on research request; defensive scanner stated to be released (no URL in text)

biases.detail: Authors' benchmark, generated by GPT-5.4, judged by GPT-5.4, used to evaluate a student distilled from GPT-5.4 traces.
Detection for LLM scanners decided by GPT-5.4 / Claude Opus 4.7 judges; no human agreement reported. Rule-based scanners are scored by a different criterion (new findings), an asymmetric metric.
n=76 headline set; the 'surpasses GPT-5.4' claim rests on one scenario.
Refinement/prefill configuration chosen with reference to the evaluation set; student is in-distribution with the attack generator.
Headline is recall only; precision 60.9% for the student surfaces only in the appendix and frontier precision is not reported.
Rule-based scanners were explicitly targeted during mutation refinement, guaranteeing low scores.

coi.affiliations: School of Electrical Engineering, KAIST (all three authors)
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Commercial scanners (Snyk Agent Scan, SkillScan) evaluated unfavorably; authors' own scanner favorably
coi.detail: Academic authors with no vendor tie, but they build both the benchmark and the winning scanner (self-evaluation rather than commercial COI).

verdict_reason: The threat (language-plus-code attacks hidden in skills) is well demonstrated and real-world transfer is checked on ClawHub, with ablations. But the defense result is self-evaluated on a small in-distribution set with LLM judges, recall-centric headline numbers, no variance, and restricted artifacts; treat the 'frontier-level 7B scanner' claim as preliminary.
applicability: Relevant if the team shares skills or SKILL.md-style instruction packs across mixed agent hosts: treat third-party skills as untrusted supply chain, pin and review them like dependencies, and do not rely on SAST/SCA or generic prompt-injection detectors to vet them. Since sensitive repos must not leak content or credentials, prefer first-party skills stored in the repos, an install-time LLM review plus human approval for new skills, and sandboxed execution of skill scripts. A local scanner avoids sending skill contents to third parties, which may matter for compliance. Nothing here is Java-specific or about multi-repo work or spec-driven development.
